world.setting: St. Petersburg, a sleepy Mississippi River town in antebellum Missouri: dusty board sidewalks, whitewashed picket fences, the county courthouse, the Sunday school room, a limestone cave in the hills above the river, and the broad brown Mississippi with its steamboats and an island of willows
world.register: period documentary realism, mid-1840s American small town, sun-bleached daylight and candlelit interiors, river and cave

tom.name: Tom Sawyer
tom.role: Mischievous, quick-talking boy of about twelve, the book's protagonist. He turns chores into games and wins other boys' treasures by persuasion; his conscience is slow but real.
tom.look: A freckled, sandy-haired 12-year-old boy in a faded blue cotton shirt with patched knee trousers and bare feet, a grin that is half mischief, a tin bucket or whitewash brush in hand.

huck.name: Huck Finn
huck.role: Tom's best friend, a ragged outcast boy whose father is a drunkard. Free of the town's rules, he is the book's most honest witness.
huck.look: A thin, barefoot 13-year-old boy in ragged homespun clothes, a battered straw hat with a torn brim, dirt on his face and a sly, watchful expression.

aunt-polly.name: Aunt Polly
aunt-polly.role: Tom's stern but loving aunt, who sets his chores and tries to keep him honest in a town of rigid respectability.
aunt-polly.look: A stout, grey-haired woman of about sixty in a dark calico dress with a white collar and apron, spectacles on a cord, a wooden spoon or a switch in her hand.

becky.name: Becky Thatcher
becky.role: The judge's daughter, the town's prized girl. Tom wins her favour with a Bible prize he bought with tickets he never earned.
becky.look: A fair-haired 11-year-old girl in a pale blue dress with a white pinafore and a ribbon in her hair, shy eyes and a careful posture.

injun-joe.name: Injun Joe
injun-joe.role: A half-Indian outlaw, violent and vengeful, who kills Dr. Robinson in the graveyard and lets an innocent man hang for it. He is the book's true predator.
injun-joe.look: A gaunt, dark-haired man in his thirties in a torn, dirty brown coat and slouch hat, a hard face with a scar, an unshaven jaw and a cold, unblinking stare.

muff-potter.name: Muff Potter
muff-potter.role: The town drunk, a poor man falsely accused of the graveyard murder, chained in the jail awaiting trial.
muff-potter.look: A ragged, unkempt man in his forties with a grizzled beard and bloodshot eyes, wearing a torn grey shirt and stained trousers, chained at the wrist.

ben-rogers.name: Ben Rogers
ben-rogers.role: A boy who is first to trade for the whitewashing privilege, a comic foil who pays Tom for the chance to paint.
ben-rogers.look: A round-faced 12-year-old boy in a grey cotton shirt and frayed suspenders, eating an apple, a cheerful and gullible grin.

sid.name: Sid
sid.role: Tom's good, obedient half-brother, who tattles on Tom whenever he can.
sid.look: A slight, neat 9-year-old boy in a clean white shirt and pressed short trousers, hair combed flat, a prim and self-satisfied face.

judge-thatcher.name: Judge Thatcher
judge-thatcher.role: Becky's father and the town's judge; presides over the murder trial with a grave sense of order.
judge-thatcher.look: A dignified man in his fifties in a black frock coat and white high collar, grey side-whiskers, presiding from a raised bench in a timber courtroom.

narrator.name: Narrator
narrator.role: The voice of Mark Twain's book, observing the town with dry irony.
narrator.look: A quiet middle-aged man with a dark moustache in a dark suit and waistcoat, leaning on a writing desk with an open book, a half-smile.

everyman.name: Everyman
everyman.role: A generic reader or townsperson, used for the argument's general claims about work, value and conscience.
everyman.look: An ordinary adult in a plain grey coat with a neutral, thoughtful expression.

street.look: A dusty board sidewalk of a small Missouri river town in summer, a whitewashed picket fence beside it, heat-shimmer in the air.

shore.look: The Mississippi riverbank at dusk, a raft tied to a willow, the broad brown river beyond, a steamboat's smoke on the horizon.

court.look: A crowded timber courtroom with a raised judge's bench, a jury box and rows of townspeople packed on hard benches, a single window of light.

forest.look: A dim graveyard of leaning wooden markers and a tall tree at midnight, lit only by a lantern, with the trunk of a dead elm and moonlight through leaves.

classroom.look: A Sunday school room with rows of wooden benches, a lectern and a Bible on it, bright windows and the smell of wax.

abstract.look: A dark limestone cave with dripping stone and a candle's small light, Becky and Tom lost in its passages, the walls closing in.

objects.why: Tom's wealth in Sunday school tickets and whitewash labour; the currency of the town's value system.
The courtroom and the judge's authority: the town's agreed justice, which convicts the wrong man.
The graveyard murder and Tom at his own funeral; death as a town rumour and a secret.
The Bible prize for memorised verses, bought with tickets: merit that is bought, not earned.
Tom attending his own funeral in disguise and the costumes of pretending.
Written tickets and the whitewash bargain's paper record of who owes what.
Muff Potter chained in the jail while he awaits a trial for a crime he did not commit.
The river road and Huck's wandering life away from the town's rules.
The Mississippi, the raft and Jackson Island, where the boys are presumed drowned.
Aunt Polly, Sid and Mary: the household that disciplines and watches Tom.
Sunday school and the day school of ruined clothes and fights.
Tom's conscience at the trial and what he stands up to protect.

spine.claim: In St. Petersburg, a boy turns a punishment into a line of people paying for the chance to work, showing that value is a story a community agrees to.
The Sunday school ticket economy rewards the look of merit: Tom buys a Bible prize with tickets he never earned, and the town applauds the appearance of virtue.
In the graveyard at midnight, Tom and Huck witness Injun Joe kill Dr. Robinson; the secret now weighs on the boys' consciences.
The town hangs an innocent man, Muff Potter, while Injun Joe walks free; Tom's silence becomes a moral cost he can no longer hide.
Tom speaks in court, the cave swallows him and Becky, and the buried gold is found: the reward for a conscience finally put to use.
